transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-11-09 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neal (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (Aperture CTO), Ethan Cole (Aperture ML Eng), Sara Park (Aperture Security), Jon Liao (Aperture Infra)

Summary (auto): customer evaluating migration from OpenAI to Redwood Dedicated for production conversational agents and embeddings. Main concerns: eval parity, latency, cost, and private deployment/security.

00:00 Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is maya from redwood, with liam our se. how's everyone doing?
00:06 Priya: good thanks, appreciate you fitting us in, we've got about 45 minutes. quick concisely — we're looking to move some of our traffic off OpenAI and evaluate dedicated infra.
00:14 Maya: perfect. quick run of who you are and what you're running today?
00:19 Priya: sure I'm priya cto, ethan runs the ml stack, jon infra and sara handles security. right now prod uses OpenAI gpt-4x for chat and embeddings via the api, about 300k tokens/day average with spikes to 2.5M/day.
00:30 Ethan: yeah and we also run some experiments on vLLM in-house for lower latency, but it's not stable for bursts and the cost math is fuzzy.
00:38 Liam: got it. are you using function-calling heavily or more free-text?
00:42 Priya: a mix, function calling for structured actions and a lot of free-form summarization. also we use a custom tokenizer pipeline — not purely off-the-shelf.
00:50 Maya: good context. top-level goals?
00:53 Priya: reduce per-token cost and get more predictable latency. also want tighter control for data residency and to integrate with our KMS. and we need SOC 2-compatibility and SSO/SAML for enterprise access.
01:05 Maya: makes total sense. Redwood Dedicated is often used for exactly that — reserved GPU pools, KMS integrations, VPC/private control plane. quick question on latency target — p95 or p99?
01:15 Ethan: p95 under 400ms for short conversations (<=512 tokens) and p99 ideally under 800ms.
01:22 Liam: that's achievable with the right model and kernel choices; we usually recommend a model profile and batching policy for that workload.
01:29 Priya: one of our big worries is eval parity — outputs we get from OpenAI baseline must match or be better. different sampling, temperature, and tokenizer wandered. can you replicate that?
01:40 Liam: short answer — we're careful to match decoding parameters and tokenization, but there are differences across model family and runtimes. if you use the same open model weights (where available) and tokenization you can get very close. some customers also keep a small calibration eval set so we can tune sampling and prompt templates.
01:56 Ethan: what about the cases where we used OpenAI's proprietary models — are there compatible Redwood-hosted equivalents?
02:02 Maya: depends. we host curated open and licensed models; for proprietary OpenAI-only flavors there's no 1:1 sometimes. but we offer fallbacks and can route to hosted models or recommend close open alternatives. for enterprise needs we can discuss how to keep some requests on OpenAI during a staged migration.
02:20 Priya: we also saw mention of vLLM and TGI in your docs — what's the difference operationally?
02:25 Liam: good question. vLLM and TGI are inference runtimes that people run themselves; they vary in batching, kernel support, and memory handling. Redwood's runtime is designed to pick kernels and batching strategies automatically for the model/hardware so you get better throughput and more stable latency under variable load. also we handle KV cache, streaming, and multi-tenant isolation cleaned up.
02:45 Sara: on security, we need specifics on KMS, key rotation, audit logs, and can you host in our VPC?
02:51 Maya: yes, Redwood Private/Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS like AWS KMS or HSM, audit logs export to your SIEM, and private control plane options. we have SOC 2 reports and a security pack we can share.
03:06 Priya: perfect. on the integration side, will our current API calls change much? we have ~100k lines of orchestration code built around OpenAI style calls.
03:13 Liam: we provide a compatibility layer and SDK that mirrors OpenAI patterns for generation and embeddings. there are some differences in model names and a few params but minimal code changes for most customers. we can provide a shim for any custom headers you need.
03:28 Ethan: tokenizer mismatch — we have a custom tokenizer. if token offsets change our downstream NER/labeling breaks. how do you handle tokenizer parity?
03:36 Liam: we can run tokenization parity tests as part of the POC. best practice is to bring your tokenizer or a spec; we can run the same tokenization in our eval harness. if needed we can containerize your tokenizer for inference.
03:49 Priya: benchmarks — we want an apples to apples comparison: cost per 1M tokens, p95 latency, and qualitative evals (ROUGE/QA pass rates).
03:58 Maya: agreed. the typical POC is 2 weeks: 1) ingest your prompts + token histogram, 2) run baseline against OpenAI using your eval set, 3) run Redwood Dedicated with tuning, 4) share results. Liam will lead the benchmark plan.
04:14 Liam: i'll include exact metrics, sample rates, and measurement scripts. question: do you want us to include streaming and function-calls in the same run?
04:22 Ethan: yes both. streaming is critical for UX. also we want to test high-concurrency bursts.
04:28 Jon: networking — for Dedicated in our VPC, what does peering look like and how much of the infra lives in our account?
04:33 Maya: for Private deployments we do a customer-managed control plane option or a VPC peering model; we can share network diagrams. some customers opt for full on-prem packages if they need air-gapped.
04:42 Sara: encryption in transit and at rest? KMS handling?
04:45 Liam: TLS in transit, and keys are customer-managed for Private instances. we integrate with AWS KMS/GCP KMS and can support rotation policies and audit log export.
04:55 Priya: onboarding timeline — assuming we like the POC, how long to go to Dedicated prod?
04:59 Maya: typical is 4-8 weeks after POC depending on compliance checks and commit size. Dedicated provisioning and tests take 1-2 weeks, then rollout and smoke tests.
05:09 Ethan: cost — what's the unit economics compared to OpenAI?
05:12 Maya: it depends on throughput and batch efficiency — for high volume customers we usually see 30-60% cost reduction versus hosted OpenAI, especially once you tune batching, caching, and quantization profiles. we'll share example TCOs.
05:25 Priya: any customers who migrated from OpenAI and kept eval parity?
05:29 Maya: yes — a couple of fintech and healthcare customers. we can share anonymized case notes and an eval sheet showing parity tuning steps.
05:38 Priya: ok great. one more: licensing — do we need to worry about redistributing model weights if we self-host?
05:44 Liam: depends on model license; for LLaMA-derivatives and some open weights there are license constraints. we can advise and recommend license-friendly model choices or host models in a way that complies with their terms.
05:56 Priya: outstanding. action items and next steps?
06:00 Maya: i'll send pricing and the SOC 2/security pack. Liam will send the benchmark plan and request for workloads. you'll send token histograms and sample prompts. then we schedule a deep-dive next week. sound right?
06:11 Priya: yes. thanks everyone.
